_source: docs/design-bible.md: Lore moments. The DM lore deck, embedded in the app and delivered only through the DM view. Edit cards here.

anchor.name: Caretaker-9
anchor.voiceNote: Leads with statement type and emotion, then the line: 'dry, faintly smug - ...'

groups.name: First Echoes
groups.description: Fire the first time a party reaches a place or milestone.

groups.name: Basalt Depths
groups.description: Fire the first time anyone drafts a named boon. Each named boon is the absorbed technique of a past visitor.

groups.name: Archival Dispatches
groups.description: Ready answers for common questions. Each one waits for the next post-boss room.

groups.name: Lost Things
groups.description: Loot, oddity and Quantum Basalt moments. Relic lore already ships with each relic, so these cover the rest.

groups.name: The Local God
groups.description: Shrines, hidden gifts and the god's own gift.

groups.name: Party Echoes
groups.description: The fall, the lockout, and the dungeon learning the party.

groups.name: The Strongest Echoes
groups.description: Fire as a boss room opens for the first time, before initiative.

groups.name: Honed Echoes
groups.description: Fire the first time anyone in the campaign levels, fuses or evolves a boon.

groups.name: Kin of Stone
groups.description: Fire the first time the party meets a creature from each family.

cards.title: Welcome, pilgrim
cards.readAloud: The stair down is lined with locals in undyed robes, and every one of them is smiling. They press dried flowers into your hands, touch your shoulders, murmur blessings in a dialect that sounds like counting. An old woman with a brass key on a string around her neck catches your wrist. "Every visitor teaches him something," she says. "Your footwork. Your fear. The way you hold your breath before a swing. Go on down. He has been waiting to learn you." Below you, the stone hums, low and pleased.
cards.push: The locals call their god Thils, true god of mazes, traps, games and lost things. They don't pray for safe passage. They pray to be interesting. Visitors are a kind of sacrament here, because whatever a visitor does in the dark below, Thils keeps a copy of it. The key around the old woman's neck opens nothing she owns. She found it on this stair forty years ago and has waited for its owner ever since, because to the locals, returning a lost thing is the holiest act there is.
cards.dmTruth: Literally true: Thils absorbs the technique of everyone who enters, which is why named boons are echoes of past striders. The locals are feeding their god, and they know it.

cards.title: Mind the Shift
cards.readAloud: At the bottom of the stair, a brass placard is bolted to a column: FLOOR ONE: MIND THE SHIFT. Fresh basalt has grown over half of it, smooth and warm, as if the stone swallowed the sign sometime this week. Chalk arrows from past tourists cover every wall, pointing in every direction at once. When you glance back, the stair you just came down has a different number of steps. Nobody saw it change.
cards.push: The chalk arrows are layered like sediment, the oldest faded to ghosts, and none of them agree. Read enough of them and a pattern shows: every arrow pointed true on the day it was drawn. The Basalts rebuild themselves every time someone leaves, floors, rooms and the things living in them, so the arrows are a record of mazes that no longer exist. Under the oldest arrow, in fresh chalk, someone has added a note: "The stones move when everyone is gone. So keep coming back, there has to be more here."
cards.dmTruth: It rebuilds only while no one perceives it. That is a thread toward the campaign's big bad. Never explain it here.

cards.title: The expedition floor
cards.readAloud: Below the first floor, the offerings stop. No more wax, no more flowers. In their place you find a survey beacon of Archive make, dented and scorched, half buried in a column that grew up around it. It still blinks. Three short, one long, three short: an Archive check-in code, the kind every strider memorizes in orientation. It has been sending that signal for a very long time, to someone who stopped answering.
cards.push: The beacon's serial plate dates it to one of the Archive's earliest expeditions into this place, older than the pilgrims' brass placards. Its last logged entry is a crossing manifest: two names, Kaelen and Vyr, and a note that "the gate is stable for crossing at dawn." No survey of this floor has ever found a gate. The entry is signed, and underneath, in a different and much shakier hand: "We are still in here. We can hear you."
cards.dmTruth: Kaelen and Vyr's expedition, now the floor 2 boss. The manifest was written before the gate broke; the second hand wrote after Thils absorbed them.

cards.title: The gate floor
cards.readAloud: Some of these columns aren't stone. You notice it by sound first: a hollow ring where there should be dead weight. Riveted struts, painted to match the basalt or grown over by it. Wipe the dust from one and there's a schematic engraved underneath in gold-veined lines: concentric rings, anchor points, a transit lens at the center. Every strider in the party has seen this diagram before. It hangs on the wall of every stride gate room in the Archive.
cards.push: The schematic is wrong in a way only a trained eye catches. Archive gates are one-way; their lenses are ground to push. This lens is ground to push and to pull: a two-way gate, which the Archive's own engineers call theoretically possible and practically suicidal. Along the bottom edge sits a maker's mark, a compass rose with one arm snapped off. Below it, scratched in a hurry, is a line of text in no language anyone knows, repeated three times.
cards.dmTruth: The Basalts is a fractured stride gate, built two-way to the meadow, then blown apart and turned inside out. The maker's mark belongs to the engineer who became the Gatewright; the scratched line is the Gatewright's phrase, "It was meant to go both ways."

cards.title: The inverted floor
cards.readAloud: Golden light falls upward from below, pouring out of the cracks between the hex tiles and throwing your shadows onto the ceiling. Grass grows up there, soft and green, and dew falls from the floor toward it. The air smells of rain and honey. Somewhere far off, birds are singing, but the song runs backward, unwinding note by note until it ends in silence. Then, for one breath, everything smells of ash.
cards.push: The grass on the ceiling belongs to no species anyone in the party has seen in any universe, and it's healthy, thriving, as if it were growing in its proper soil under its proper sun. Only the direction is wrong. Press an ear to the floor, and under the hum you hear wind moving through tall grass, a great deal of it, rolling over open country. And something enormous, very far away, breathing slowly in its sleep.
cards.dmTruth: The meadow on the far side of the gate is bleeding through, inside out. The breathing is the Sun-Eater's Husk, or something like it, still partly on the other side.

cards.title: Quarantine
cards.readAloud: The comms crackle without warning, and for the first time since you entered, there's no delay. An automated Archive voice, flat and fast: "Hazard class revised. Previous: Black. Current: Quarantine. All striders in the affected zone are advised to withdraw." Then nothing. Then, late as ever, Caretaker-9: "Alarmed, uncharacteristically sincere - I have never seen that rating on a place people go on purpose. I am not telling you to come back. I am noting that I would like you to."
cards.push: The alert carries metadata, and anyone who can read Archive traffic can pull it apart. Quarantine has been assigned only a handful of times in the Archive's history, always to the site of a breach, a place where one universe has torn open into another. The zone it covers isn't the floor you're standing on. It's a point a little below it, small and very bright on the scan, pulsing in the same rhythm as the beacon on floor 2.
cards.dmTruth: Floor 5 sits on the gate's ruptured core. The matching rhythm hints that the expedition's beacon and the core are part of the same system.

cards.title: Ulma's Thread
cards.readAloud: As you take it, a red thread pulls taut from your wrist and runs back through the rooms behind you, straight as a plumb line however the corridors bend. It hums when you face the way you came. Then a voice, hoarse and furious and very close, as if someone has her mouth pressed to the stone: "Three times, you smug stack of pebbles. Three times I walked out of here. Keep the trick. I'm coming back for the rest of you." The thread goes slack, and the voice is gone.
cards.push: Ulma Unar, called Ball of Yarn, is a Master of the Pale Lodge's Order of the Tracker. She is the only Lodge member, past or present, to walk out of the god's maze with her target relic in hand, and she has done it three times. Whatever happened to her in there curdled into hatred. She now recruits anyone who will help her kill Thils, and most of the Lodge laughs about it. The members who know her don't. One of them says that if she needs the Mazekeeper dead, she won't stop until she has split his skull.
cards.dmTruth: Thils took her technique anyway, an insult she doesn't know about yet. If the party ever meets Ulma and tells her, it could recruit them into her crusade.

cards.title: Travert's Echoes
cards.readAloud: Your strike lands, and half a second later the stone rings like a struck bell, one pure clean note, and the note hits the target again. You feel it in your teeth. Somewhere in the walls, a man laughs, delighted, the laugh of someone who just won a bet he made with himself years ago. "Twice," he says. "Always twice. Once for them, and once for the song."
cards.push: Archive entry logs list a Travert, a percussionist from a world where music was a martial art, who registered as a strider so he could "hear how other universes ring." He believed every surface had a note, and that if you struck it right, the note would strike for you. His last log was filed from the pilgrims' stair: "Going down. Heard it's the best acoustics in the multiverse." He never filed another.
cards.dmTruth: Thils absorbed his technique. His tuning gauntlet waits in Thils's Vault; the gauntlet's second ring is the part of Travert that Thils couldn't keep.

cards.title: Elemain's shots

trigger.label: First draft of any Elemain boon

cards.readAloud: Your shot goes wide and keeps going. It bends around a column like it's looking for something, turns once, twice, and buries itself in a target you hadn't spotted yet. From somewhere behind you comes a woman's voice, utterly bored: "Told you. Never twice." Then, quieter, almost fond: "Mind the ricochet. It holds grudges."
cards.push: Elemain was a bounty archer from a world of floating islands, where a missed shot fell for a mile and was gone for good. She trained until her arrows simply didn't fall. Lodge records list her as a freelancer who took contracts on targets nobody else could find, because her shots kept hunting after she stopped. She claimed she had never missed twice. Her last contract sent her into the Basalts after a target the slip described as "unhittable." She went to prove it wrong.
cards.dmTruth: Her ricochet ring is in Thils's Vault, still warm. Whatever the unhittable target was, she never came back to collect.

cards.title: Lenn's Descent
cards.readAloud: A plumb line unspools from nowhere, a brass bob on waxed cord, and drops past your feet into a hairline crack in the floor. The cord keeps feeding out. Ten feet. Fifty. It falls far longer than the floor is thick, until a reel you can't see clicks empty and the cord hangs taut and trembling. Something at the bottom tugs it twice, politely, like someone asking to come up.
cards.push: Lenn was a surveyor, the kind the Archive sends ahead of an expedition to measure what a place really is. Her rule was simple: never trust a floor until you know what's under it. She dropped her line into every pit, shaft and stairwell in the Basalts, and her notes record depths that keep growing. Floor one, ninety feet. Floor two, three hundred. The last entry is a single number with far too many digits, and then four words: "Not a dungeon. A throat."
cards.dmTruth: The cord came back up without her. The Basalts go deeper than five floors; the gate's core sits at the bottom of a shaft no one has measured, drawing things down.

cards.title: Corrow's Lure
cards.readAloud: Something tugs at the edge of your mind, gentle as a hook through cloth. Not pain. An invitation. For a moment you can feel every dead end you've walked past on this floor, and in one of them, small and cold, a presence that has been lost for a very long time. The hook says: this way. Come on. I've got you.
cards.push: Corrow was a fisher from a drowned world who made a living, and later a calling, of pulling lost striders out of the maze's dead ends. The locals still tell stories about him; some of them say their families exist only because Corrow reeled in a great-grandparent. He was endlessly patient and would wait days at a dead end for someone who might never come. In the end, the stories say, he felt a tug on his own line from somewhere deeper than any dead end, and he followed it down.
cards.dmTruth: Thils collects lost things, and eventually he reeled in the fisher. The tug Corrow followed was Thils.

cards.title: Ostra's Coin
cards.readAloud: A coin spins on the floor in front of you, though no one dropped it. It's heavy and old, one face serene and sleeping, the other a grinning skull, and it spins without slowing, humming, never quite deciding how to land. When you reach for it, it's already in your palm. Warm on one side. Cold on the other.
cards.push: It echoes the Token of Whim. Whim was a single-plane true god of the endless cycle of life and death, imprisoned beneath the Pewter Citadel and kept alive by the Tri-Planar Trade Alliance so they could siphon its power. Ten thousand cycles past its time to die, with its home universe rotting from the imbalance, Whim took out a Pale Lodge contract on itself, rated 11.2. The reward for setting it free was a two-sided coin that can, once in a hundred cycles, raise one of the dead or end one of the living.
cards.dmTruth: (proposed) Ostra was the hunter who fulfilled that contract and carried the Token into the Basalts. The real Token is somewhere in Thils's collection.

cards.title: Pog's Path

trigger.label: First time Pog's Path is earned

cards.readAloud: For a moment the room becomes lines on paper. Every column is an inked circle, every exit a gap in the line, drawn fast and still wet, the pen racing ahead of you. You see the room from above, like a map. Then the ink runs, the lines blur and drip, and the room is just a room again. But your feet remember where the floor was true.
cards.push: Pog, Wanderer of the Underways, is a senior Tracker of the Pale Lodge who specializes in hostile terrain and recovering lost items, and only takes contracts rated 4 to 8. He's known in the Lodge for one boast: any labyrinth can be mapped if you draw faster than it changes. He went into the Basalts to prove it. The Lodge still lists him as active and available for hire. Nobody has actually seen him in years.
cards.dmTruth: Pog's unfinished map is in Thils's Vault; Awoken, it finds the way out of a god's own labyrinth. (proposed) Pog is still alive somewhere deeper, still drawing.

cards.title: Zolic's Nine Eyes

trigger.label: First draft of Zolic's Nine Eyes

cards.readAloud: Something behind your eyes grinds into focus, a lens turning in a socket you didn't know you had. The world sharpens. The enemy in front of you suddenly has seams: weak points, the places where it was put together. You count without meaning to. One eye open. Eight to go. And at the back of your head, a low voice, patient as a hunter in a blind: "Again."
cards.push: Zolic of the Nine Eyes is a senior Hunter of the Pale Lodge, one of the few who takes contracts for titan-killing, the slaying of false gods and demigods, and the nullification of true gods. He ground each of his lenses from the eye of something larger than a world, one lens per kill, and wears them in a ring around his skull. Eight eyes. The ninth socket has been empty for a long time. He says he's saving it for something worth looking at.
cards.dmTruth: The ninth eye was meant for one more hunt. (proposed) That hunt is Thils, which ties Zolic to Ulma's crusade.

cards.title: Thalisane's Weave

trigger.label: First draft of Thalisane's Weave or Weaver's Mending

cards.readAloud: A thread of shimmering light spins out of nothing and ties you to an ally, wrist to wrist. For a moment you feel their heartbeat beside your own, out of step, then in step. Their pain is a dull ache in your own arm. Someone wove lifelines here, a long time ago, so no one would fall alone. The thread still remembers how.
cards.push: Thalisane, wielder of the Shimmer Staff, is a Master of the Pale Lodge's Order of the Weaver, which handles search and rescue, life weaving, hex removal and emergency extraction. She went into the Basalts on a rescue contract carrying a shuttle of light and came out with every hunter she went in after. It's the only perfect extraction from the god's domain in the Weavers' records. She has never said what it cost her.
cards.dmTruth: She got out alive; her shuttle didn't. That was the price. She could turn up in the campaign wanting it back.

cards.title: Re: Thils

trigger.label: Answer to a question about Thils

cards.readAloud: Patient, lecturing - "Thils. True god, multiplanar, which means he exists on more than one plane at once and is not inconvenienced by any one of them burning down. Portfolio: mazes, traps, games and lost items. The Pale Lodge calls him a collector. His worshippers call him the Mazekeeper. I call him a hoarder with better marketing. He is very old, very patient and very interested in you specifically. I find that last part the least comforting."
cards.push: Pull the file further and it gets stranger. Thils's domain holds thousands of relics, some of them famous, all of them lost by someone first. He doesn't steal. He waits. Anything misplaced near enough to his domain finds its way in eventually, and once it's his, it stays his. Even relics he gives away come home: anything from his Vault sold for credits returns to him. Caretaker-9 adds a footnote: "This includes people. Please do not get lost."
cards.dmTruth: Canon from the Pale Lodge broadcasts.

cards.title: Re: Getting out

trigger.label: Answer to a question about escape or exits

cards.readAloud: Grim, unusually brief - "Lodge field notes on Thils's mazes agree on one thing. The only reliable way out is the exact passage you came in by. Not a similar passage. Not the passage that is now where that passage used to be. That one. Do not lose your way back. I would have to file paperwork, and I would have to mean it."
cards.push: Most people who can't find their way back don't die. That's the part the Lodge leaves off its contract boards. They wander until they stop wandering, and then they settle. Deep in the god's domain there are cities, generations deep, built by the descendants of treasure hunters who never found their door again. Some of them name their streets after the passage their ancestors came through. Some still keep a candle burning beside it.
cards.dmTruth: Canon: the god's labyrinth holds generational cities of the never-escaped. (proposed) The locals on the pilgrims' stair descend from one, which is why they revere the god who keeps them.

cards.title: Re: Lethality

trigger.label: Answer to a question about danger or the Lodge

cards.readAloud: Dry, faintly smug - "The Pale Lodge rates every contract by lethality, on a scale where a 2 is a bad afternoon and a 15 is a god. The ratings assume the rater did their homework. I am told their raters occasionally sandbag a number to fill a contract faster. I am told this by the families of junior hunters."
cards.push: One story in the Lodge's complaint records stands out. A junior hunter named Roteus was sent after the sword of Apo on a contract rated 6.2, because the rater had heard Thils was in a dormancy cycle. Thils was awake. Every trap twice as deadly, every beast three times as mean: the honest number was 12 at least. The rater spent the next day trying to hire anyone at all to go in after Roteus and quietly fix it. Nobody knows how that ended. The Lodge closed the complaint as resolved.
cards.dmTruth: Canon (the Lore Machine story). Roteus's contract slip can turn up as loot in The contract slip.

cards.title: Re: Devotions

trigger.label: Answer to a question about Devotions or the locals

cards.readAloud: Curious, earnest - "The locals call your progress Devotions. Every room you clear, every technique you prove, counts as an offering. Archive researchers agree something is being given down there. They disagree, loudly and in print, about who is giving it to whom. One paper is titled Who Is Training Whom. It has forty-one rebuttals."
cards.push: The minority view in those papers is the unsettling one. Every visitor leaves stronger, measurably. But the Basalts get stronger too, in exactly the ways their visitors did. A sword technique proven down there on one day shows up in a stranger's boon draft a week later. The researchers who hold this view have a nickname for the dungeon: the mirror that keeps the reflection.
cards.dmTruth: Both are true. The party grows, and Thils learns them as they do. Their own techniques can become someone else's boons.

cards.title: Thils is awake

trigger.label: Party chooses two or more Pressures for the first time

cards.readAloud: Concerned, clipped - "Lodge chatter says Thils sleeps in cycles, long ones, and that contracts in his domain are priced for a god who is dreaming. When he wakes, every trap gets meaner and every beast gets hungrier. The locals' hymns are louder today. Two of them were seen weeping for joy. Draw your own conclusions. I already have, and I have written them down in case they are needed later."
cards.push: The locals have a phrase for the waking: the god leans in. When he leans in, they say, he isn't angrier. He's interested. A sleeping Thils collects whatever wanders in; a waking Thils plays. The pressures you chose didn't make the dungeon harder on their own. They're a god pulling up a chair, because someone finally made the game worth watching.
cards.dmTruth: Canon: awake, his traps are twice as deadly and his beasts three times as mean. Pressures are the in-world sign of a waking god, which is why they pay more.

cards.title: The contract slip

trigger.label: Any loot reveal on floor 2 or deeper

cards.readAloud: Among the loot, a scrap of heavy paper, torn and water-stained, stamped with the Pale Lodge's seal. A contract: retrieve the sword of Apo, legendary hero of the Aranphere, for an unnamed client. The lethality rating, 6.2, has been scratched out so hard the pen tore through. Beside it, in shaky handwriting, someone has written 12 and underlined it three times.
cards.push: The back of the slip is covered in a junior hunter's notes, written smaller and smaller as the paper ran out. Directions, crossed out. A tally of days. A sketch of a sword hanging point-down over a pedestal, behind a door with no keyhole. And at the very bottom, barely legible: "If you find this, tell the overseer the rating was wrong. Tell him I didn't run. Tell him I found it."
cards.dmTruth: Roteus's slip. The Sword of Apotheos is real and waits in Thils's Vault. The door with no keyhole is oddity 3. (proposed) Roteus may still be alive in one of the maze's cities.

cards.title: Something of yours

trigger.label: Oddity 1: an item a player lost long ago

cards.readAloud: On top of a column, alone, sits {item}. It's exactly as you left it the last time you saw it, years ago and somewhere else entirely. The same scuff. The same smell. There's no dust on it. Someone has been keeping it clean.
cards.push: Look closer and it's been cared for: polished, mended where it was broken, a thread wound tight around the worn spot. A small tag is tied to it, carrying one word in the locals' handwriting: "Returned?" The question mark looks like it was written very carefully, by someone who has been hoping for a long time.
cards.dmTruth: Thils collects lost things, all of them, even small ones from other universes. Before the run, ask the player what they once lost, and fill {item} in. Taking it back is allowed; the locals will cheer.

cards.title: The first Basalt
cards.readAloud: The shard is warm, warmer than your hand, and heavier than it looks. Under the light it isn't black at all. Every color is in there, folded up small and turning slowly, like a storm seen from very far above. Hold it to your ear and you can almost hear something. Travel. The feeling of a step that hasn't landed yet.
cards.push: Quantum Basalts sell for a thousand credits apiece anywhere the Archive's economy reaches, and the striders who carry them report the same odd side effect: a faint pull, like a compass needle, toward the last stride gate they used. Archive assessors classify them as crystallized transit energy and politely decline to say where that much transit energy would come from.
cards.dmTruth: Crystallized stride energy from the gate's core, the same energy the Stride Core sheds.

cards.title: A shrine to Thils

trigger.label: First shrine to Thils in a room

cards.readAloud: A knee-high cairn of hex stones stands against the wall, heaped with offerings: stubs of wax, pressed flowers and small lost things. A key on a ribbon. A child's shoe. A single earring. A pair of spectacles with one lens missing. In front of it, a prayer is carved into the floor, so fresh the stone dust hasn't settled.
cards.push: The prayer reads: "Keeper of what is lost, here is something lost. Keep it, or let it find its way home. Either way, see that it was loved." The locals don't leave treasure here. They leave the things they found and couldn't return, trusting Thils to do it for them. Every so often an offering vanishes, and somewhere, in some universe, someone finds a thing they lost years ago sitting on their doorstep.
cards.dmTruth: Hidden condition 12 rewards an offering made mid-fight, if the shrine survives. (proposed) Thils really does return some lost things; it's how he keeps his worshippers.

cards.title: Thils approves
cards.readAloud: The moment the condition is met, the hum in the stone changes key. Somewhere in the walls, something chuckles. Not cruelly, not mockingly: the way a game master laughs when the players finally try the thing they were supposed to try three sessions ago. Warm air moves through the room like an exhale. Then one word, felt more than heard: "Good."
cards.push: Anyone watching closely catches the condition itself, written briefly in gold light across the floor before it fades. Thils shows you the rule only after you've followed it. He isn't hiding the game. He wants you to learn it the way he learned you: by watching what works.
cards.dmTruth: Thils is playing with them. He wants to be beaten in interesting ways, and his gifts reward clever play over brute force.

cards.title: Thils's Favor

trigger.label: First Vault opening, Thils shrine, room condition met, room trick sprung, or hidden boon with no card of its own

cards.readAloud: The hymns humming through the stone stop. All of them, at once. For one breath the whole floor holds still, the way a crowd goes quiet when someone important walks in. You feel attention settle on you, enormous and amused and not unkind, like being picked up and turned over in very large, very careful hands. Then the hymns start again, louder than before.
cards.push: Every other boon in the Basalts is borrowed, a technique Thils took from someone who came before you. This one isn't. The locals have a saying: a favor is the only thing Thils gives that was never someone else's first. Pilgrims wait their whole lives for one. Some of them weep when they hear that a tourist got one on a first visit.
cards.dmTruth: The only boon that's the god's own gift rather than an echo.

cards.title: Expelled
cards.readAloud: You don't fall. There's no impact and no darkness. You're simply set down, gently, outside on the pilgrims' stair, the way a misplaced item gets returned to a front desk. Your pockets are lighter. Your Basalts are gone. When you try to go back down, the steps just keep going, and after a while you're standing where you started. The locals bring you tea. None of them look surprised.
cards.push: An old man sits down beside you on the step. "He doesn't kill you," he says. "He keeps what you showed him and sends the rest home. You'll be let back in when he's finished studying you." He pats your hand. "Most people find it flattering, eventually."
cards.dmTruth: (proposed tie-in) The lockout could double as Archive quarantine for striders who die inside. Thils keeps a copy of how they fell, and it may turn up in someone's draft.

cards.title: Your echo

trigger.label: Oddity 2: an echo of a party member walks past

cards.readAloud: Across the room, someone walks past mid-fight with something you can't see. It takes a moment to recognize them, because it's you, or someone wearing your stance, your scars, your bad habit with your left foot. They're using a trick you haven't learned yet. It works. They never look at you. Then they turn a corner that isn't there and they're gone.
cards.push: The echo's gear is yours, but scuffed differently, worn in places yours isn't yet. Whatever you just saw wasn't your past. The Basalts have watched you fight long enough to guess what you'll become, and they're practicing it. Whoever drafts that trick someday, maybe you, maybe a stranger a hundred years from now, will be borrowing it from a version of you that never existed.
cards.dmTruth: Thils is learning the party. One day their technique may be someone else's boon. If the player likes, hint at a future boon for their character.

cards.title: The Tessellated Warden
cards.readAloud: A hive of hexagonal columns heaves itself upright, grinding, settling into something with shoulders and arms. Gold-veined runes crawl across it, pulsing slowly, like breathing. In its chest, behind a cracked lens, there's a still image: a sunlit golden meadow, perfectly calm, the grass caught mid-ripple in a wind that will never finish blowing.
cards.push: The runes are Archive transit script, the same lettering painted around every stride gate frame in the Archive, but written backward, as if meant to be read from the other side. They spell one instruction, repeated: hold the frame, hold the frame, hold the frame. The meadow in the lens isn't a painting. Stare long enough and a single blade of grass moves.
cards.dmTruth: Built from the original stride gate's outer frame. The meadow is the universe on the far side of the gate, frozen at the moment it broke.

cards.title: Choir of the Hollow Column
cards.readAloud: The room is a forest of fluted basalt pipes, some taller than a house, some no thicker than a wrist, and all of them are humming. As you step in, the hum gathers into a chord, and the chord into words, sung by a hundred voices that aren't there: the pilgrims' hymn from the stair, every verse at once. The pipes turn toward you like heads in a choir loft. The last note swells until your ribs ache.
cards.push: Every pilgrim who ever sang on the stair is in here somewhere. The basalt keeps sound the way other stone keeps heat, and for generations the locals have sung their god's hymns down into the dark. The pipes grew around the echoes. Listen past the chord and single voices come through: a child getting the words wrong, an old man singing flat and not caring, a woman who stops mid-verse to laugh. The Choir isn't angry. It's performing, and it has never had an audience that sang back.
cards.dmTruth: The locals' devotion given a body. (proposed) If the party sings the pilgrims' hymn back, the Choir falters, and the fight could end in harmony instead.

cards.title: Gilded Excavation Herd
cards.readAloud: Something enormous and patient plods into the room: an Archive survey golem, the old boxy kind, so overgrown with golden crystal it glitters like a reliquary. Two basalt hounds trot at its heels on tethers of light, sniffing the floor, then lifting their heads toward you in perfect unison. A stenciled work order is still legible on its chest plate: EXCAVATE TO FOUNDATION. It lowers its digging arm and starts toward you, as if you're standing on the foundation.
cards.push: The golem's serial number belongs to the same early expedition as the beacon on floor 2. It was sent down to dig, it never received an order to stop, and so it never has. The golden crystal choking its joints is warm and smells faintly of honey, and it grows thickest on the side of the golem that faces down. Whatever it was digging toward, it got close enough for something to grow on it.
cards.dmTruth: An excavation golem from the gate's original construction, still digging toward the core. The gold crystal is the meadow's light, set hard. The hounds are Wardstones Thils gave it for company.

cards.title: Kaelen and Vyr
cards.readAloud: Two voices, one flickering silhouette, talking over each other in the clipped rhythm of a log being read into a recorder. "Log entry four-one-one, gate stable, crossing at..." "...crossing at dawn, gate stable, log entry four-one-one, Kaelen speaking..." "...Vyr speaking..." The silhouette splits into a heavy vanguard and a sniper sharing one shadow. They both look at you. "Are you the relief team?"
cards.push: The log numbers match the beacon on floor 2: these are the two names on its crossing manifest. Kaelen was the expedition's vanguard and Vyr its marksman, and by every Archive record they were inseparable, partners for twenty-two strides. They were the first through the gate on the morning it failed. Whatever pulled them in took them together and never bothered to separate them.
cards.dmTruth: Absorbed by Thils. Their final log was recorded before the gate broke, and they don't know it broke. If the party tells them, the fight could change.

cards.title: Halvard Quill
cards.readAloud: A tall figure in a long pale coat flickers into place like a bad projection, a contract slip in one hand and a pen in the other. He reads the slip, then looks up and runs his eyes slowly over each of you, the way a buyer looks over cattle. He stops at your weakest member, smiles, and ticks something off. "There you are," he says.
cards.push: Lodge records list Senior Tracker Halvard Quill as dead on a contract inside the Basalts, rated high enough that only Seniors and above could take it. His colleagues remember a trapper who never fought fair and never apologized for it. The slip he's holding has a name on it. Anyone close enough to read it sees the name of whoever in the party is most hurt right now.
cards.dmTruth: An absorbed echo, still working his last contract on whoever fits it. (proposed) Bringing his Lodge tags back could earn a commendation.

cards.title: The Lattice Spinner
cards.readAloud: Cables crisscross the room from column to column, thick as your arm and humming with blue-white current, strung so densely the air looks woven. In the middle of the web, something unfolds: a great many-limbed spider built from cable and cracked crystal lenses, each lens a different eye, each eye fixed on a different one of you. It plucks a single cable. The note travels the whole web and lands in your teeth.
cards.push: The cables are transit lines, the kind the Archive strings between anchor points to hold a stride gate open while it's in use, and they're still carrying load. The Spinner isn't spinning a web. It's maintaining tension, restringing every line that snaps, tying the room together the way these lines once held something far bigger together. When a cable breaks, it doesn't flee or strike. It repairs first. It was built to hold, and no one has told it to let go.
cards.dmTruth: Built from the gate's tension cables and shattered transit lenses. Like the Blind Architect it keeps things in place, but the Spinner is only following its last instruction.

cards.title: The Stride Core
cards.readAloud: A sphere of light hangs over a grated floor, the size of a house and far too bright to look at straight on. It breathes. Every few seconds it surges, a pulse of pressure that squeezes the air from your lungs, and then it settles. When it settles, crystals form on its shell: black, glittering, every color folded up inside. Quantum Basalts, growing like frost and falling through the grate like hail.
cards.push: This is where Quantum Basalts come from: raw stride energy, the force that carries a strider between universes, leaking out of something and cooling into stone. But stride energy doesn't pool. It flows from a gate to its destination and is gone. For this much to collect, something would have to be open and going nowhere, a door held ajar for a very long time, pushing and pulling at once, with nowhere to send what passes through.
cards.dmTruth: A fragment of the gate's core, still trying to finish a crossing that broke mid-transit. Every Quantum Basalt the party has spent is a crystallized piece of a journey that never arrived.

cards.title: General Vane of the Tenth Stride
cards.readAloud: A suit of basalt armor stands at the end of the hall, three times the height of a person, and as you enter it turns its helm toward you with a sound like a landslide. From inside comes not one voice but hundreds, perfectly in step, a whole platoon calling cadence: "TENTH STRIDE. HOLD THE LINE. TENTH STRIDE. HOLD THE LINE." The General raises a stone sword, and a hundred voices raise it with him.
cards.push: Vane was a multiplanar conqueror whose armies marched between universes by force. He heard a rumor, old even then, of a door somewhere that led to a world with no winter, no hunger and no war, and he brought the Tenth Stride, his finest platoon, to take it. They found the Basalts instead. On the third floor, the dungeon folded the whole platoon into one suit of armor to save space. They've held the line ever since, against an enemy that never comes, guarding a door they never found.
cards.dmTruth: Vane came after the gate broke, chasing rumors of the meadow. He's an absorbed echo of an entire army; the cadence is every soldier at once. (proposed) A soldier's name called out by the party might break step.

cards.title: The Glass Hydra
cards.readAloud: The floor here is fused glass, swirled and bubbled like the inside of a furnace, and from a crater at its center something rises on many necks. Crystal heads, each a different color: one smoking red, one crackling white, one frosted blue. Light passes through the creature and comes out bent, so its shadow falls in several directions at once. When it opens its mouths, the sound is glass under strain.
cards.push: Gate-glass forms in only one place: where stride energy hits a surface at the wrong angle and fuses it on the spot. Archive engineers find a few beads of it after a bad crossing. This crater is gate-glass all the way down. Something here broke in a single enormous flash, and the shockwave froze into a beast. Count the heads and count the colors. They match the light that spills from the gate schematic on floor 3 when you hold a lantern to it.
cards.dmTruth: Grown from gate-glass where the core first ruptured. The crater is ground zero of the explosion.

cards.title: The Blind Architect
cards.readAloud: A shape made of nothing stands at the far wall. Not darkness. Nothing: a hole in the room, edged by shards of basalt that turn slowly around it like moths. It kneels at a seam in the wall where gold light is leaking through and, with great care, smooths it closed, the way someone mends a tear in a favorite coat. It has no face. It turns toward you anyway.
cards.push: The shards orbiting it are the same basalt as the walls, but cut precisely along the lines of the gate schematic from floor 3. It isn't attacking the dungeon. It's maintaining it. Every seam it closes is a place where the far side was leaking in. Whatever it is, it's working very hard to keep this place broken in exactly the way it's broken now.
cards.dmTruth: The dungeon's closest brush with the campaign's big bad. Who it works for stays unsaid.

cards.title: The Chorus of Unseen Angles
cards.readAloud: At first the room looks empty. Then you catch it at the corner of your eye: a shape like a cut gem made of nothing at all, hanging in the air. Turn to look and it's gone, and now there are two more, at the edges of your sight, always just where you aren't looking. The hymns that hum through the rest of the Basalts are missing here. Not quiet. Missing, like a word you know you know.
cards.push: The locals' hymns name every room of the dungeon, every floor, every boss. Every room but this one. Ask a local and they'll start to answer, stop, frown and change the subject. The silence isn't avoidance. Something here was removed, a piece of the dungeon or of the god who keeps it, cut out so cleanly that even Thils doesn't seem to know it's gone. The shapes aren't creatures. They're the outline of the hole.
cards.dmTruth: Where the campaign's big bad ate away part of Thils's memory. Never explain it; this is as close as the deck gets.

cards.title: The Inverted Reliquary
cards.readAloud: The vault doors stand open, but they open inward, onto the room you're standing in, as if you're already inside the vault and the treasure is out there somewhere. Shelves line the walls, crowded with reliquaries, every one of them empty and scrubbed clean. Warding runes run across every surface, glowing a soft temple gold. As you step forward, they turn toward you all at once, the way a lock turns toward a key.
cards.push: This was the heart of the locals' temple, the vault where they kept Thils's holiest lost things until their owners came for them. Its wards were written to protect what was inside. Then, on some Shift long ago, the vault came back facing the wrong way, and the wards never noticed. They still guard the vault against what's inside it, and now everything is inside it. They've erased every relic it held, one by one, and now they're turning their attention to you. The locals still bring offerings to its door.
cards.dmTruth: The temple vault, landed inside out on a Shift too near the core; its wards now erase whatever they hold. (proposed) The erased relics weren't destroyed. They're the lost things Thils can no longer remember, which ties the Reliquary to the Chorus.

cards.title: Ophaniel of the Inverted Bloom
cards.readAloud: It fills the arena: a being of wings and rings and golden glass, half a vast and beautiful beast, half a living cathedral, its ribs arched like a nave and its eyes set in wheels that turn and turn. It should be the most beautiful thing you have ever seen, and it almost is. But every part of it faces the wrong way: petals folded inward, light pouring into it instead of out, wings spread to shelter something behind it that isn't there. When it speaks, its voice is a choir singing welcome, backward.
cards.push: There's a shape to its welcome, if you listen long enough: the cadence of a greeting rehearsed for one very special day. It isn't guarding the gate. It was sent to the far end of the crossing to meet the first travelers from this side, to fold its wings around them and bring them in out of the light. It was halfway through that embrace when the world turned inside out, and it's still holding the shape of it. Its arms are still waiting for someone to fill them.
cards.dmTruth: The Long Meadow's herald, sent to greet the first crossers and caught in the gate the instant it broke. The someone it was meant to embrace was Kaelen and Vyr.

cards.title: The Sun-Eater's Husk
cards.readAloud: The arena is half skeleton, half mountain. A colossal leviathan lies fused into the bedrock, its golden antlers branching across the ceiling like the roots of an upside-down tree, its hide cracked open in places over a light so bright it burns. It's only half here. Its back half disappears into the stone, and through the stone you can feel it breathing on the other side. It lifts its great head and looks at you with the slow curiosity of something that has never once been afraid.
cards.push: In the Long Meadow, the Sun-Eaters grazed on light the way cattle graze on grass, drifting across the sky in herds and leaving gentle dusk behind them. This one wandered too near the crossing on the morning the gate broke and was dragged halfway through. It has been starving ever since: half its body lies in a world full of sunlight it can't reach, and the other half is buried in the dark, eating every light that comes near. It isn't cruel. It's hungry, and you brought lanterns.
cards.dmTruth: Dragged halfway through the gate as it broke and fused into the bedrock. Its back half is still in the Long Meadow, which is the breathing heard on floor 4.

cards.title: The Gatewright
cards.readAloud: It turns, and its face is a thousand faces, each blinking at a different time, mouths moving out of step. Its hands are an engineer's tools, welded in place and still turning, still adjusting. Behind it the arena keeps rebuilding itself into rooms you've already fought through. "It was meant to go both ways," it says, in all their voices at once. "It was meant to go both ways. We were almost there."
cards.push: Among the faces, a handful wear Archive survey gear older than anything issued today. Most wear clothing no strider recognizes, cut for a warmer sun. These are the first minds the gate took, swallowed whole before Thils learned to keep only what was useful. At the center sits one face that never blinks, an engineer still checking measurements, still certain the gate can be finished if the numbers are run one more time.
cards.dmTruth: Aurelin Vey, the engineer who designed the gate, fused with its core and the thousand minds it swallowed before Thils ever found it (see The whole story). "Almost there" means the gate was seconds from opening both ways when it failed.

cards.title: A boon deepens

trigger.label: First time anyone levels a boon

cards.readAloud: As the boon deepens, the echo inside it comes into focus. For a moment you aren't borrowing a trick. You remember learning it: a training yard you've never seen, a teacher's voice you've never heard, saying "Again. Again. Better." Your hands know the weight of a weapon that isn't yours. Then the memory folds itself away, and the technique is a little more yours than it was.
cards.push: Every boon is a copy of someone's technique, and the copy gets better the more it's used, because Thils's copies aren't perfect. Each strider he learns from teaches him more of the same skill, the way a dozen witnesses describe one face. When your boon levels, you aren't just practicing. You're filling the gaps in the copy with yourself. Somewhere in the stone, the record of the original strider has quietly been updated to include you.
cards.dmTruth: Leveling writes the player's own technique into the echo. This is how the party ends up in other people's drafts.

cards.title: Two echoes meet

trigger.label: First time anyone makes a Fusion

cards.readAloud: Two techniques meet in your hands and don't fit, and for a moment you feel them argue: two strangers' habits, two ways of standing, two people who were never in the same universe, let alone the same fight. Then one of them laughs, the other gives way, and they find a rhythm together. Somewhere in your head, two voices that have never met say at the same time: "Oh. Like that."
cards.push: The striders behind your boons never knew each other. Some died centuries apart, in universes that will never touch. In the Basalts they're kept side by side, and when you fuse their techniques, you make them meet for the first time. The locals consider a fusion a small miracle and a kind of matchmaking. Some pilgrims come down just to fuse two boons and hear the echoes introduce themselves.
cards.dmTruth: Fusions are Thils's favorite thing to watch: something new made from two lost things. (proposed) A Fusion could become an echo of the party in its own right.

cards.title: A technique finished

trigger.label: First time anyone evolves a boon

cards.readAloud: The boon breaks open into something its owner never managed. You feel the echo behind it reach the edge of everything they knew, and then you feel yourself go past it. There's a long pause in the stone. Then a voice, the original strider's, very quiet: "That's what I was trying to do." It isn't jealous. It sounds like someone setting down something heavy after carrying it a very long way.
cards.push: An evolution is a technique finished. Every strider Thils absorbed was cut off mid-practice, mid-idea, mid-fight, and their boons hold the shape of what they were reaching for and never caught. When you evolve one, you catch it for them. The locals say the echo can rest after that, though no one knows what rest means for a copy. Pilgrims who witness an evolution light a candle at the nearest shrine, the way you would at a funeral that's also a graduation.
cards.dmTruth: Evolving a boon completes an absorbed strider's unfinished technique. It's the closest thing to peace the echoes get.

cards.title: Wardstones
cards.readAloud: Hexagonal columns pull themselves out of the walls and floor, shaking off stone dust like dogs shaking off water, and settle into shapes: a squat hexling, a hound with an ember-slot for a mouth, a sentinel taller than the doorway. Gold runes wake on their faces, all reading the same word in the locals' script. They don't charge. They step between you and the room's far exit and wait, the way doormen wait.
cards.push: The word on the runes is Keep. Wardstones are Thils's own servants, carved from the dungeon's basalt, the oldest guardians of his labyrinth. They don't hate intruders. They keep things: rooms, exits, the order of the maze. When they step into one column and out of another, they're using paths only the keepers know. The locals carve little wardstones from fallen chips and set them on their windowsills, the way other people keep a picture of the family dog by the door.
cards.dmTruth: Thils's guardians, set on the broken gate's doors when he took it in. They're the only thing in the Basalts that was made for it on purpose.

cards.title: Mazework
cards.readAloud: The room is full of things that shouldn't move. A chest with too many hinges. A coat hanging on a hook with no wall behind it. A doorway that wasn't there a minute ago and is now considerably closer. Something big and horned waits at a corner, perfectly still, until you look straight at it. Then everything in the room moves at once, and none of it was ever furniture.
cards.push: Mazework is what happens to traps and lost things that sit in Thils's labyrinth long enough. A trap set and never sprung starts to resent the waiting. A lost thing no one comes back for learns to go looking on its own. The god of games and traps takes a quiet pride in them: his collection, learning to play. That's why they arm a trick when they fall. Even their last move is a setup.
cards.dmTruth: Thils's collection come alive. Everything Mazework becomes was lost or set by someone once; a sharp party might recognize a piece of gear from a relic's story.

cards.title: The Lost
cards.readAloud: It takes a long time to notice them, and that's the worst part. A figure at the edge of the room in a pilgrim's robe gone grey. Another sitting against a column, so still you'd walked past it twice. Their faces are hard to hold onto: look away and you can't remember them, look back and they're closer. One of them opens its mouth to say a name, and stops, because it can't remember whose.
cards.push: The Lost are people who came into the god's labyrinth, never found their door again, and stayed lost so long the world forgot them. Their families stopped looking. Their names fell out of every record. The locals say Thils keeps everyone who's lost, but these are the ones even he stopped thinking about, the things at the very back of the collection. They aren't hunting you. They're following you, because you're the first thing in a long time that looked at them.
cards.dmTruth: The forgotten. Being overlooked is what made them this way, a quiet thread toward the campaign's big bad. (proposed) Remembering one by name, from a relic or a note, could give it peace.

cards.title: Absorbed Echoes
cards.readAloud: Silhouettes flicker into the room like a projector warming up: striders in gear from a dozen universes and a dozen centuries, translucent at the edges. They move with a confidence you recognize. One of them steps exactly the way your fighter does. One casts with the same flick of the wrist as a boon you drafted two rooms ago. They don't speak. They nod to you, politely, like colleagues. Then they attack.
cards.push: Every strider Thils learns from leaves a copy in the Basalts. Most copies are only a technique, kept for drafting. Some are more: whole habits, whole fighting styles, a ghost of a person built around the trick. Those are the Echoes. They aren't the striders themselves, any more than a recording is the singer. They fight with one borrowed boon because one boon is all they are. The locals treat them kindly. Some of their ancestors are among them.
cards.dmTruth: Copies of past visitors built around a single absorbed technique. A fallen party member could appear as one in a future run.

cards.title: Gate-Born
cards.readAloud: The air tears with a sound like ripping silk, and things step out of it: a wisp of white fire humming a single note, a cat-shaped thing standing in two places at once, a golem of swirled glass with something bright trapped in its chest. They leave scorched pools of light wherever they walk, and the light doesn't fade. Looking at them feels exactly like the moment in a stride when you've stepped through and haven't landed yet.
cards.push: The Gate-Born were never alive and were never anywhere else. They formed here out of raw stride energy and gate-glass, the way crystals form in a cooling cave. Their force is transit force, the push that throws a strider across universes, with nothing to throw. Archive engineers would know the signature at once. They'd also tell you it's impossible: stride energy only collects this densely where a gate has been open, and stuck, for a very long time.
cards.dmTruth: Born of the gate's leaking core. They're the most direct physical evidence of what the Basalts really is.

cards.title: Inverted Paradise
cards.readAloud: Golden things come out of the light. A dryad whose leaves curl inward, toward the trunk. A unicorn with its horn turned in, pointing at its own heart. A tall figure with wings folded the wrong way, like a robe worn inside out, and a face so serene it hurts to look at. Everything about them is beautiful, and everything about them faces the wrong way. When one of them reaches out to heal a companion, the companion screams.
cards.push: Nothing here was born in the dark. Every one of these creatures comes from somewhere bright and gentle, a world of open country and long gold afternoons where healing was the most natural thing there was. They came through the gate in its last moment and were turned inside out, so that what mended now harms and what harmed now mends. They aren't evil. They're homesick, and they're still doing exactly what they always did, in a world that runs backward.
cards.dmTruth: Ordinary life from the Long Meadow, caught in the gate's last moment and turned inside out. Not monsters: neighbors.
